Your file says you rebuilt the planning side of the company. Tell me about the team you built, and start with the hardest decision.
The hardest decision was a hire. In 2019 I brought in a planning engineer from outside the family, and I put her above four foremen who had been with us for twenty years.
Why her, and not one of them?
None of them had the skill set. Our schedules were always late, and the delays were due to planning, not to the work on site.
How did the foremen react?
Badly, at first. Two of them stopped talking to her, which is why I onboarded her myself and sat in on her meetings for two months.
And what did that hire lead to, in the end?
Our delays fell by a third in the first year. As a result, the foremen started asking her for the schedule, and staff turnover on the sites dropped too.

When I ask a candidate about a team he built, most people give me an organization chart. Twelve engineers, three foremen, one assistant. That tells me the size of the team, and nothing else. What I am really listening for is cause and consequence. Why did you hire this person and not that one? What happened as a result? A strong answer connects every decision to what it led to. The second thing I listen for is the people who left. Every real team loses somebody, and staff turnover is a normal part of building anything. If a candidate tells me that nobody ever left his team, I do not believe him, or I suspect that he never asked anybody to change. The third thing is simple. I want to hear one person by name, somebody you hired or promoted, and what that person is doing today. Because of that one detail, I can usually tell whether you built the team, or only inherited it.

Early in my career I made a hire I was very proud of. I poached a brilliant engineer from our biggest competitor, and I paid him almost twice what my other engineers earned. On paper he had the perfect skill set. In practice he was not a cultural fit. He made every decision alone, and he never explained anything to the younger engineers. As a result, two of them resigned in the same month, and the team lost more knowledge than he had brought in. The problem was not really him. It was the reason I hired him. I had looked only at his technical record, and not at all at how he worked with people. Since then, every candidate for a senior role spends a full day on one of our sites with the team before we make an offer. It takes longer, and we lose some good people because of it. But in the last five years we have not had to replace a single senior hire.
